source_text: Verum non uno modo vicisse con tentus, argumenti tui, cuius impietatem prodidi, coarguam falsitatem. Cum ergo scriberes: Non ideo potuit oriri voluntas mala in opere Dei, quia a Deo factum est; sed ideo quia de nihilo factum est [n75] ; videre debueras, quam valenter aliarum creaturarum exempla praescriberent, quae totidem productae de nihilo, malae tamen voluntatis capaces non sunt. Postremo ipsa elementa, quae vere sunt facta ex nihilo, non alicuius voluntatis conscientiam queunt habere, ut motibus malis protestentur originis suae necessitatem. Animantes autem, et reliqua queis impletus est orbis, non de nihilo, ceterum iam ex aliquo prodierunt. Ubi est ergo vis inanitatis antiquae, quae malam voluntatem coegit existere; cum praeter rationabile animal, neminem peccare posse manifestum sit?
pass_a_gloss: But not content to have conquered in one manner, I will convict of falsehood your argument, whose impiety I betrayed. When therefore you were writing: Not therefore could an evil will arise in a work of God, because it was made by God; but therefore because it was made from nothing; you ought to have seen how valiantly the examples of other creatures would prescribe, which equally produced from nothing are nevertheless not capable of an evil will. Finally the elements themselves, which truly were made from nothing, cannot have a consciousness of any will, so that they would protest by evil motions a necessity of their origin. But living beings, and the rest with which the globe is filled, came forth not from nothing, but already from something. Where therefore is the force of the ancient emptiness, which compelled an evil will to exist; when it is manifest that besides a rational animal no one can sin?

LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Not content to win in only one way, I will expose the falsehood of the argument whose impiety I have revealed. When you wrote, ‘An evil will could arise in God’s work not because it was made by God, but because it was made from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48), you should have seen how powerfully the examples of other creatures argue against you. They too were brought forth from nothing, yet are incapable of an evil will. Indeed, the elements themselves, which truly were made from nothing, can have no consciousness of any will, so as to attest through evil movements the necessity of their origin. Living creatures, however, and the other things filling the world, came forth not from nothing but from something already existing. Where, then, is the power of ancient emptiness that compelled an evil will to exist, when it is clear that no being except a rational creature can sin?

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian contrasts opportunity/help with imposed necessity; load-bearing against natural compulsion to sin.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
